newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Good track record needed for EMU - Schmidhuber.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Good track record needed for EMU - Schmidhuber.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Peter Schmidhuber said on Friday that nations wanting to join the single currency must have a good track record of stability and a final spurt to the 1997 finish was not good enough.

Nations seeking to join Europe's planned monetary union in 1999 must show they have pursued stability-oriented policies in past years and that they have reached the required level of lasting convergence, he added.
This was important for the success of the single currency, the euro, Schmidhuber said in a speech to a German-Dutch conference in Ebenhausen, in the state of Bavaria.
"Hectic" attempts to meet the deficit criteria were causing only the appearance of convergence, and that appearance was being enhanced by speculation in the capital markets.
Countries which want to join EMU in the first round in 1999 must meet a series of economic targets this year. For most, the fiscal policy goals have proved the hardest to reach.
But a number of countries, notably Italy and other southern European states, have made strong efforts this year to meet the agreed targets.
Schmidhuber said that if bond yields of a country fall because capital markets expect it to join EMU that had nothing to do with convergence, "but is the result of speculative investment decisions."

He also said that while a stability pact agreed to ensure lasting fiscal discipline after monetary union was important, its effect would be limited if a country failed to keep its budget spending on a tight rein and there was a dispute.
"One-off shows of strength in budget policy already carry the seeds of a fall back into fiscal laxity," Schmidhuber said.
"Cooking the books and creative accounting must be prevented as far as possible.

"For a successful start of the euro it is important that the currency union only begins with those countries which can prove they have pursued stability policies in past years and have reached the required degree of lasting convergence."
Accepting countries which had failed to convince the European public or financial markets that they were stability-oriented would burden monetary union from the start, Schmidhuber said.
Schmidhuber also called on European governments to demonstrate notable progress in further European integration or risk losing the support of the general public for the integration process.
He said it would be critical for the so-called Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) -- a year-long meeting of European Union government officials -- to show some progress in this respect.
"The European Council meeting in Amsterdam in June 1997 should reach fundamental decisions regarding the IGC or even complete it," Schmidhuber said.
"One can only hope that the Dutch presidency will suceed in achieving a respectable result," he added.
The IGC is intended to address political issues related to further European integration as well as to set the blueprint for the admission of additional states to the 15-nation group.
